title: WHAT IS IT ABOUT FIRSTBORNS?
raw_text:
Does birth order really matter? Dr. Kevin Leman contends it profoundly affects us, whether we realize it or not. "The family constellation shapes the social behavior of man," states Psychologist Karl Konig. "It determines the way he reacts to other people, how he is able to make friends or not, the way he finds companionship. Even the choice of a husband or wife is deeply influenced by the family constellation."

While the influence of birth order on our behavior can be overstated, that doesn't mean there is none. It's probably not simply a coincidence that of the first 23 astronauts in space, 21 were firstborns and two were onlies. Firstborns tend to display patterns of strengths and weaknesses:

* Firstborns tend to be cautious individuals who take calculated risks, as opposed to leaping into the unknown.
* They tend to be analytical and logical.
* They tend to be reliable since they've been held to a higher standard by getting more individual attention from their parents.
*They tend to have a strong sense of right and wrong.
* They are the perfectionists trying to live up to their parents high expectations.
* They are either pleasers who don't know how to say no, or controllers, especially if they are males with younger brothers.
* Natural leaders, their slogan is, "I'll take care of that for you."
* They are disproportionately movers and shakers who end up as top managers and CEOs.

They have weaknesses as well. "Firstborn males struggle to relate to others," and if they have younger brothers, may have trouble understanding women, writes Leman. Firstborns, especially males, also tend to have fewer good friends than last-and middle-borns.

Leman offers advice on mitigating firstborn weaknesses. They tend to have fewer good friends due to being too opinionated, which works against developing friendships except with those who share the same opinions, and they jump right in to solve problems, though others sometimes just want to be heard or to connect and don't like know-it-alls. Instead, firstborns should resist their black-and-white thinking, let friends find their own solutions, and lighten up and refrain from criticism.

If they are pleasers, Leman recommends that firstborns learn how to say "Let me think about that." And to later make a call saying, "No, I'm not able to help this time, but thanks for asking."

Perfectionists can be discouraged from trying something because they fears they can't do it without mistakes. It's healthier to recognize that no one can be perfect at everything.

Conscientious, responsible people can get overscheduled and overworked. Firstborns need to schedule fun and seek balance.

Controllers may be achievers, but sacrifice relationships to win. Reduce the harm this way:
* Listen before giving orders to see a task from the other person's viewpoint.
* Reign in the criticism by realizing that others need not live up to the firstborn's high expectation for herself.
* Ignore minor details that others don't do as well as you.
* Delegate and trust others to do the job, even when you suspect others won't do it as well as you. Firstborn Jimmy Carter worked himself into exhaustion by refusing to delegate.
* Treat everyone as important, not as merely a cog in the plan.
* Inspire others to perform at their peak potential because they are respected and considered valuable members of the team.

Why are firstborns different? Because they enjoy parental attention without competition, typically getting thousands of more hours of parental quality time than subsequent siblings. They have the biggest photo albums, Leman writes, and parents who overreact to what they do. Parents often place higher expectations on them. Firstborns are more likely to internalize the standards they grow up with.

This book will be of interest primarily to firstborns. Leeman gives much less attention to middletons and last-borns in this book. Readers can find more about subsequent siblings in his earlier work, The Birth Order Book, An interesting point he makes, however, is that almost all comedians are last-borns such Jay Leno, Jim Carrey, Drew Carey, Whoopi Goldberg, Chevy Chase, Stephen Colbert, Ellen Degeneres and so on. They also make top salesmen due to high social skills.

What the book lacks is acknowledging other factors in personality development. It is nevertheless and enjoyable and quick read. ###

title: beautiful and eerie
raw_text:
Notes from Ghost Town was beautiful and eerie, and a great read. It's a wonderful and bittersweet read, one that I was hesitant to read at first (though I really don't know why), but loved when I finally picked it up.

Sixteen-year-old Olivia has just flunked out of art school. Returning home, she stumbles through all the memories of her best friend, Stern, and of his murder. They say her mother killed him, and her trial is to take place in little over a week. Then Stern returns as a ghost, muddling through incoherent memories and convinced that her mother wasn't his killer. And, together, they race to put together all the little fragments of rumor and memory to find out what really happened the night Stern died.

Olivia was an interesting character, and one that was easy to understand. Stern's death left her color blind, and when she first saw his ghost, she immediately thought that she had schizophrenia like her mother. She thought she was going insane. She copes with everything as best she can, struggling through it all as best she can. She wasn't particularly feisty or strong, nor was she spineless or a pushover, but rather in-between like many are, and it's really easy to connect with her.

The last time she spent with Stern before he died in particular tugged at my heart, when she realized she loved him as more than a friend, but couldn't quite tell him at the time, and then never got the chance. There's so many scenes in Notes from Ghost Town that's beautifully written and really makes you feel like you're there in that moment with the characters, entering a party or walking down the beach or driving away from Ghost Town, and I loved it.

The mystery and the buildup was perfect. I loved how even the most random little things, at the end, had a purpose. Olivia follows so many false leads and hits her fair share of dead ends and moments of frustration before finally piecing everything together, and in the end it all comes together. There's just enough suspense to keep you on the edge, waiting, waiting, waiting...

Stern and Austin were interesting enough to read about, a boy in Olivia's past and a boy in Olivia's present, but at times, they felt a little like the same person. The before-Stern and Austin, I mean. Ghost-Stern was a jumble of fragmented memories, and was nothing like Austin. I think it was something about the way they spoke and moved that made before-Stern and Austin seem so similar to each other. Just something I noticed while reading, though it didn't make for any confusion of any sort.

abbreviated.

PROS: The writing; Olivia; everything had a purpose; the feeeels.

CONS: Not really a con, but before-Stern and Austin felt similar in a way.

OVERALL: Notes from Ghost Town was a wonderful novel, with a great main character, beautiful writing, and a great end. All the little parts of the novel worked so well with each other. It was a great story, and now I have to get myself a copy of The Butterfly Clues, Kate Ellison's first novel.

title: Adequate, barely, for a beginner who wants never to improve
raw_text:
I purchased this book for a non-birder friend who had asked for something easy to use. I knew I wasn't getting a serious field guide, but still, I was stunned at how poorly set up this book is. Any book that uses photographs instead of paintings (and no more than two per species at that) starts out with a big problem, and any book that isn't meant to be comprehensive is already inadequate for serious use, but this author compounded both of those weaknesses by making an egregious error: He organized the book not by taxonomy, nor shape, nor even habitat or anything else useful, but by COLOR. Yes, color, the least useful aspect of a bird for identification purposes (but the one to which every beginner defaults). This means that similar and related birds aren't anywhere near each other -- even males and females of the same species are in entirely different places. You can't turn to the ducks, or the herons, but only to the mostly-brown birds, the mostly-black ones, and so on.

I realize that beginners will think that's a good idea; heck, my friend loves the book. But anyone using this will be inclined not to learn birds at all, but to leaf through the book, sometimes finding something that looks superficially correct (and often not finding any match at all, as color varies so much in the field and if the user doesn't decide what the primary color is -- and don't think that won't happen, as for example every non-birder focuses on things like white bellies) and thinking (s)he has learned something, but this book is essentially designed NOT to lead beginners to a greater understanding of anything, and will in many cases just produce frustration.

The book will attract many novices... and that's unfortunate.

This book is interesting in several different areas.

I initially picked this up because I was interested in learning about Dave Pallone's story about his struggle to keep his homosexuality a secret in order to keep a job he loved, back in the 70's through the '80's when the sports world had no place nor tolerance for those who had a "deviant" sexual orientation. And it was a hard story to read about. He could NEVER relax his guard or take for granted anything about the possibility his private life becoming public. His relationships had to ALL be kept undercover. He writes about it well enough that I got a nervous stomachache in sympathy for him as I experienced his tension and worry right along with him.

Within a few chapters I also became interested in his professional life as a baseball umpire. I am mostly indifferent about baseball but he managed to capture my attention and keep my interest as I learned what it takes to be a sports official in general and a baseball umpire specifically. But additionally, he had not only a difficult personal life, he also had a harrowing professional life, made that way by the very people he had to work closely with and who wouldn't hesitate for a second to stab him in the heart and twist the knife if they even suspected his secret life. He crossed a picket line in '79 from the minor leagues, a crime to die-hard unionists worse than murder. It took YEARS for most of those strikers to finally accept him, and some NEVER did, even 10 years after the incident. Fortunately though, he was able to make a few good and loyal friends with mature and civilized people. Then, finally, in the late '80's, by some sneaky and underhanded dealing on the "inside," he was let go from the job that he loved, even through all the mental and emotional harassment he had to deal with in performing it. Most of us wouldn't have the mental fortitude to continue on a path that held so many obstacles and such open hateful, unfair treatment from an entire organization, but he STILL loved that job and he communicates that love in every paragraph. Highly recommend this book.

title: A sad mess. Where were the editors?
raw_text:
I found this book directly after reading [[ASIN:0778737071 Cleopatra's Coin (Stories of Great People)]], an interesting and informative book by the same authors. Published just one year later, this is a confusing and disappointing entry in the Stories of Great People series.

The book starts with a two page spread describing and illustrating Mr. Rummage's stall at Knicknack market. It is identical to the written description of Mr. Rummage's stall at the beginning of Cleopatra's Coin, but the accompanying illustration is different. The redundant text is puzzling and completely unnecessary, because this time, Digby Platt's purchase doesn't come from Mr. Rummage's stall, but from Colonel Karbuncle, an elderly gentleman who sells military uniforms, medals, flags, swords, helmets, and cannon balls from the trunk of his old jeep.

Digby is accompanied by his older sister, Hannah, who has "secret doubts about the value of Mr. Rummage's objects" and feels "for some big-sisterly reason" that she has "to stop her little brother from buying useless pieces of junk." (Page 8.) Once again, this is completely irrelevant to the story that follows, because Digby is buying from Colonel Karbuncle, not Mr. Rummage. This time, Hannah does refrain from sneering at Colonel Karbuncle's story and sniping at her brother, so the dysfunctional family dynamics I objected to in Cleopatra's Coin are mercifully absent in Julius Caesar's Sandals.

The bickering is replaced by sloppy editing, which is why I've given this book such a low rating.

On page 13, we learn that Julius Caesar married Cornelia, the daughter of a politician in the Popular party, and refused to divorce her when Sulla, the ruler of Rome and opponent of the Populars, tried to force him to do so. No more mention is made of Caesar's marital bonds until page 31, when he abandons Cleopatra and returns to his wife Calpurnia. Huh? What happened to Cornelia, not to mention Caesar's second wife Pompeia? By leaving out Cornelia's death, Caesar's marriage to and divorce from Pompeia, and his final marital union with Calpurnia, the authors confuse their audience instead of enlightening it. And Cleopatra's Coin never mentions that Julius Caesar abandoned Cleopatra---the reader is left with the impression that they were parted when Julius Caesar was assassinated. Which version is true?

On page 30 of Julius Caesar's Sandals, Cleopatra has herself "smuggled into Julius Caesar's heavily guarded rooms wrapped in a bedroll." But in Cleopatra's Coin, she was "wrapped inside a rolled up carpet." (Page 20.) So which story is correct? On page 32 of Julius Caesar's Sandals, Colonel Karbuncle talks about "Marcus Antonius" who is called "Mark Antony" in Cleopatra's Coin. Since both books are in the same series by the same authors, wouldn't it make sense if the facts and names were consistent from one volume to the next?

As in Cleopatra's Coin, the fictional part of the story---Digby and Hannah Platt's chat with Colonel Karbuncle---is printed on white paper. The historical sidebars about Julius Caesar and his world are printed on tan graph paper. In this book, though, the sidebars are sometimes very poorly matched with the text of the story, and are therefore quite confusing. For example, on page 30, the Colonel tells the children that Caesar defeated the armies of Ptolemy, Cleopatra's younger brother, and his body was found floating in the harbor the next day. But a historical sidebar on page 31 describes how Caesar's rival Pompey presented himself at Ptolemy's court, asking for men and arms so he could challenge Caesar. Ptolemy wished to placate Caesar, so he presented Pompey's head to Caesar as a gift. By page 32, we're back to Colonel Karbuncle's story, which describes Caesar's displeasure at Pompey's dishonorable death. But that must have happened before Ptolemy's death on page 30! So the fictional story is told in a non-chronological order, which is rather confusing, and the interruption of the story by the historical sidebar does little to clarify matters.

Near the end of the story, Mr. Rummage, who periodically interrupts the Colonel's tale to interject additional information, briefly describes Caesar's assassination. Digby concludes, "I wouldn't want to be in his shoes. But all the same, I'll take the sandals, Mr. Rummage." The only problem is that Mr. Rummage isn't selling the sandals---they're being sold by Colonel Karbuncle!

Now, ancient history is not my area of expertise, so I have no idea whether Cleopatra's Coin or Julius Caesar's Sandals is the more factually accurate book. I do know that while I found the former entertaining and coherent, the latter contains gaps and internal inconsistencies that left me scratching my head, hence the low rating.

title: Enjoyed it
raw_text:
Enjoyed it and would give the book 3.5 stars. The title of the book says it all. There were so many secrets, I'm surprised The Black House didn't explode with everything it was hiding. I didn't love any of the characters. Desi got the life she picked, so how can she be surprised she's in a loveless marriage where both are unhappy. She chose a man for security instead of love, because she wanted a life where she could build her own company. Desi just seemed checked out from her family and always chose work over them. I'm pretty sure Peter just stayed with his wife to make her miserable. Jules was quite annoying. She turns eighteen and declares herself an adult. She has never worked a day in her life, lived a life of privilege and has always gotten everything she ever needed or wanted. It felt like she was throwing a temper tantrum when it came to college. I would have been just as annoyed with Lenore as Desi was during their dinner. I never knew what was going to happen at The Black House, with the animal attack and horrific accident. You would think that kids that grew up in the woods would know how to act around wild animals. The girl from Chicago was the only one who knew what to do.

Definitely recommend the book. It's full of family drama and huge secrets. I can't believe Desi was able to keep the truth hidden for so long. It was almost like reading a soap opera that took place in a mansion in the wildness of North Carolina. Enjoyed the story, writing style and the characters (even though I didn't like them, they brought the drama.) Look forward to reading more books by the author.

I received a complimentary copy of this book from St. Martin's Press through NetGalley. Opinions expressed in this review are completely my own.

title: A hidden star
raw_text: It's quite a tragedy that Casey never completed a novel before committing suicide. This collection of his works (some translated into English for the first time) is an amazing taste of his burgeoning style. Casey was a friend of Virgilio Piñera and Severo Sarduy, so I was eager to read these stories. He created tight worlds that convey much in their brevity. Stand-out stories for me include "Homecoming" (where a man returns to Cuba where he's arrested and tortured for unknown reasons), "The Execution" (similar to "Homecoming" where a man is arrested for a crime he didn't commit, and yet he never speaks a word in his defense), and "Piazza Margana" (which is a brilliant love story in the style of Piñera or Poppy Z. Brite). Some stories are difficult to fathom, and yet it's evident the potency Casey had in his writing, especially when writing about his Cuban heritage and his ambivalent sexuality.

title: Great story in a small package
raw_text:
I have to admit that I was a bit shocked at how much I enjoyed reading this book. Not because its alternative history, because that is one of my favorite types of fiction. I am shocked that Mr. Heller was able to fit so much story into such a small package. The book is only 145 pages long, 161 pages if you count the afterword. I could see Conroy or Turtledove doing the same story in 600 pages!

The author begins the story with the historical break point clearly defined and accurate up to Wilhelm deciding not to invade France by way of Belgium. That such a minor difference could have such incredible repercussions is itself the story. The level of his research is evident in its historical accuracy. I especially like how he uses historical figures as the main characters in the novel.

I have few negative comments. There are only a handful of typos. It sometimes feels more like an outline than a novel. I would have loved seeing more character development with a broader narrative. This story could have easily been 500 pages, with the possibility of a couple of sequels. Japan with its own Vietnam war. Germany versus US and British Commonwealth. This book raises many questions. What would Hitler be without a defeated Germany to inspire? Would the US rise to the challenge of a European alliance? Does the Ottoman Empire fall apart? What about the Austro-Hungarian Empire?

I look forward to reading more by Andrew Heller.

title: A valuable source
raw_text:
A READER'S GUIDE TO BLOOD MERIDIAN is just what the title proclaims, providing a comprehensive glossary for all of the difficult terms, translations of the novel's many foreign words and phrases, and much of the lore behind the novel's historical characters and places.

Shane Schimpf provides an overview first, which includes a Nietzsche-derived interpretation of the novel. While this interpretation is as valid as any, and might seem handy for college students, readers should be aware that it is not the only interpretation. Just one of many. I wish that Mr. Schimpf had provided notations of the alternative published arguments or else had toned down or omitted this part of it and let readers choose their own interpretations. A guide should simply be a guide.

There follows the heart of the book, in an easy-to-read font. An examination of the epigraphs is followed by a page-by-page, chapter-by-chapter annotation of the novel. Many of the entries are brief, but often he pauses to give short biographies or extended explanations. There is a handy subject index followed by a bibliography of sources. New readers and college students will find this an immensely valuable and enlightening work.

The author acknowledges his debt to John Sepich's NOTES ON BLOOD MERIDIAN, the standard authority on McCarthy's masterpiece since 1993, and this more accessible volume will likely reach a much wider audience.

No work such as this is definitive, as the author freely admits, and a second and revised edition of this work is almost inevitable somewhere down the line.

title: This is a beautifully written memoir about the heartbreaking but riveting journeys of ...
raw_text:
This is a beautifully written memoir about the heartbreaking but riveting journeys of a suburban New Jersey well-poised family facing the unthinkable and unimaginable: the dreadful diagnosis that their son, age eight, suffers from Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD)- a rare and genetic life-threatening illness we seldom have heard of.
Jesse Torrey does an amazing job as she painstakingly confronts her bewilderment, details her unrelenting efforts and frustrations to understand the nature, scope of the disease and decides on its controversial and risky treatments. She takes us along with her and her family into their ins and outs during ten agonizing years where we witness the son's progress from his stem cell transplant to young adulthood. Despite the trauma and many emotionally haunting experiences such as recognizing that one would never be able to hear the son's voice except in dreams, the book is a celebration of life, family and a supportive community. Confronting ALD, normalcy in a family landscape is almost non attainable. Resiliency, support, understanding, love, laughs and humor do play an important role in healing and keeping families together.
But the book is much more than the intimate diary of a family coping with a life-threatening disease and resolute to do whatever needed for the survival of a loved one. It is about awareness, self-discovery, family and networking. It is informative and educational. It stands as a first-account reference and source for any parent concerned about developmental changes in a child, about seeking help when behavioral symptoms are incorrectly categorized under the broad topic of ADHD, and about how to navigate the diverse institutions and organizations, from specialized hospitals to schools for special needs, that can assist families. A book every parent should read.

title: Pratchett is the Master.
raw_text:
Holy smokes, this book was adorable.

This isn't my first Pratchett book, but I don't remember much of the one Discworld book I read back when I was thirteen or so. I do remember it being humorous - I just didn't remember how absolutely hilarious Pratchett is. I'm serious. This guy has a penchant for making people laugh and sometimes I found myself laughing so hard that I had to shut the book and put it down for a bit to recover. My flatmate found this endlessly amusing.

The characters in this book were the epitome of what it means to be lovable. Everyone from Jewish Solomon to the smelly Onan to the rich-but-will-always-be-single Angela were fleshed out and created solely for the purpose to be loved. I especially liked that Pratchett also included real people from this time. People like Robert Peel, Sweeny Todd, Benjamin Disraeli and even the well-known Charles Dickens. I can't be sure that's how those real people would've behaved in the circumstances that our hero, Dodger, always found himself in, but I loved seeing their reactions - especially Dickens's. The reader also gets to meet the Queen herself when she is young and first starting as ruler of England. This might have been my favorite part. I felt like I was being let in on some little secret by "being" with all of these people who were once real, by having these adventures with them.

I can think of no one better to write about Victorian London than Pratchett. He doesn't try to romanticize the hardships for you. He doesn't try to make it seem like this beautiful and idyllic place. He just gives you the facts - the facts from the rich people and the facts from the poor - and the facts from those caught kind of in the middle. Dodger finds himself, accidentally, caught in the middle of a diplomatic problem, something that, as a tosher, he really just wants nothing to do with. But because there's a damsel in distress (and no good Christian boy would leave a damsel in distress, would he?), he finds himself drawn deeper and deeper into the problem and the reader gets to experience his discoveries and epiphanies.

Highly recommended for everyone

title: Not for beginners
raw_text: The intended audience of this book is mathematicians who already know differential geometry. It is definitely not for beginners. It is terse and contains no figures to aid the reader's intuition. Few motivations are given and no applications are discussed. I would have expected the author to make every effort to help a wider audience - also non-mathematicians - to become familiar with the important ideas contained in his book. But no - teaching is clearly not one of his strengths. Anyone who would like to learn geometric algebra and calculus on their own would be advised to start with other books, such as (1) Doran & Lasenby, "Geometric Algebra for Physicists", (2) Alan MacDonald, "Linear and Geometric Algebra" and "Vector and Geometric Calculus", (3) John Snygg, "Clifford Algebra - A Computational Tool for Physicists" and "A New Approach to Differential Geometry using Clifford's Geometric Algebra". But unfortunately also these books are either too brief, too terse, or lacking in other ways. A really good introduction to geometric algebra and calculus for physicists is still missing.

raw_text: Harlow Giles Ungere's Lafayette is a wonderful story that relates how a young boy, courageous and determined, helped Americans such as I to gain our independence. He relates how Lafayette failed to control the French Revolution, simply because he hadn't spent enough time with Washington to learn the craft of governing. `'In rejecting political and military power, Lafayette's political ineptitude was matched only by that of the king....'' All of which led to a political vacuum which permitted the entrance of madmen such as Danton and Robespierre. But what can be done when we're assured in Lawday's Danton and Scurr's Robespierre that both men believed wholeheartedly in the power of the people, that the rich should be taxed to pay for the poor, and that the poor should be protected at all costs, that all power should be placed in the hands of the people, when this same people murdered the king's guards, the Black Musketeers, boys from age twelve; when they beheaded a baker who had nonetheless worked all night to provide bread for the mob that murdered him; when the people, mostly illiterate swine, dropped their pants to defecate in any available space, like errant dogs? The massacres continued and Danton and Robespierre's heads finally, fortuitiously, fell into a basket as filthy as the ambient dung heaps. The French then went on to accept an emperor, followed by more kings and other emperors, until the French Republic finally came into existence. All unsettling events. But still more unsettling is how another free people, the English, can still, in their vast majority, consent to live under a silly gaggle of royals, a democratic people who count for little unless they or their relatives or friends or acquaintances have the luck of being invited to their king's/queen's garden party. Anyway, Ungere's excellent book gives a wonderful overview of the American and French Revolutions--it is truly a five-star winner. My own books can be found on Amazon under Michael Hone.

All of which led to a political vacuum which permitted the entrance of madmen such as Danton and Robespierre. But what can be done when we're assured in Lawday's Danton and Scurr's Robespierre that both men believed wholeheartedly in the power of the people, that the rich should be taxed to pay for the poor, and that the poor should be protected at all costs, that all power should be placed in the hands of the people, when this same people murdered the king's guards, the Black Musketeers, boys from age twelve; when they beheaded a baker who had nonetheless worked all night to provide bread for the mob that murdered him; when the people, mostly illiterate swine, dropped their pants to defecate in any available space, like errant dogs? The massacres continued and Danton and Robespierre's heads finally, fortuitiously, fell into a basket as filthy as the ambient dung heaps. The French then went on to accept an emperor, followed by more kings and other emperors, until the French Republic finally came into existence. All unsettling events. But still more unsettling is how another free people, the English, can still, in their vast majority, consent to live under a silly gaggle of royals, a democratic people who count for little unless they or their relatives or friends or acquaintances have the luck of being invited to their king's/queen's garden party. Anyway, Ungere's excellent book gives a wonderful overview of the American and French Revolutions--it is truly a five-star winner. My own books can be found on Amazon under Michael Hone.

There was quite a bit of whining (whinging as the Brits say) that wore fairly thin. But the Guernsey setting (islands in the English Channel, occupied by Germany during WWII) was of interest, although I wish there'd been more of that and less of Deborah.

The plot involves a wealthy islander found dead on a beach -- with a rock in his throat as the cause of death. Two Americans who have just delivered a package to him are the chief suspects as far as the police are concerned. Since one of the Americans is an old friend of Deborah's, she and her husband St. James end up in Guernsey trying to prove that she (and her brother) had nothing to do with the death.

Not a bad mystery, but not a very good one either, and definitely a disappointment coming from this talented author. I didn't like the reader, an Englishman whose American accents were execrable (bad beyond belief) and who insisted upon pronouncing Cherokee (the name of one of the Americans) with the accent on the last syllable. I couldn't do that if I tried, and I kept wanting to correct him.

I wonder what the story is behind this book -- if it was an early work that she tried to do a rewrite on but that basically just wasn't very good.

When it isn't a household item, there is a Radio Shack number or other explanation of where to get it.

The plots are excellent. There's suspense and sometimes they have to hide in the basement to figure out what to do next. I never get bored. There are some terms that I didn't know until I asked my mom, such as "Occam's Razor," so I have learned a lot from reading these. I'm in 6th grade. I think they would be good for 4th grade and up but a lot of kids might have questions about some of the terms. But that's okay. That's how you learn!

These books are so funny I keep reading them out loud to people. Some parts I like to read several times in a row because it is so funny I can't stop laughing.

The citations are occasionally apt and insightful, but more often his contentions must be tortured and contorted in order to shape them to a very obvious contemporary political agenda. Claiming that Richard III is "all about winning," or that he just wanted to "make England great again" is really pretty juvenile. Almost as concerning: since when do scholars claim, without qualification, that they know exactly what Shakespeare was thinking, what he believed, and precisely what he was saying, on and off the stage?  I would have been shouted down in grad school for such pretentious overreach, but perhaps Greenblatt is channelling The Bard, who told him to get that "upstart crow," Donald Trump, through this slight, petulant, and disappointing book. I don't have a dog in this fight; I didn't vote for either of the major party candidates in our late, lamented election, but I wish that Greenblatt had resisted these childish urges, and heeded a loftier muse.  Discretion may not be the better part of valor, but I hope this nasty piece of work doesn't do too much damage to the author's reputation, and he does not come to reflect: " O, I have lost my reputation! I have lost the immortal part of myself, and what remains is bestial."

The story line has so many facets that this book will be running through my mind for a long time.

title: Wonderful Diverse Essay Collection
raw_text:
I'm not very familiar with the essay genre, so I was a little concerned that this wouldn't be the right fit for me. After the first few pages, however, I was hooked on the story and the author's writing style!

The handful of stories/essays in this book take place in China, the most populated country in the world. Because there are so many living there, Chinese are often thought of as a number and not as individual people. The author, however, tells the fictional, but seemingly realistic stories of individual men and women in this country. From the "Hotline Girl" to the woman who sells flowers, the reader is given a perspective into the every day lives of ordinary citizens.

I loved the short stories and felt that the characters were well-developed by the first few pages of the story. There is just enough irony and satire in the essays to make the reader smile and able to relate to the protagonist's flaws. This is a quick read, but that doesn't mean the stories won't stay with you long after you turn the last page.

Engaging, beautifully written, and haunting, I recommend this book to anyone looking for a diverse essay collection.

Dr. Alford was kind enough to participate in our Sesquicentennial of Booth's capture in Caroline County, Virginia. He is as excellent a speaker as he is a writer. Hearing his talk, I was even more motivated to read the book that added amazing depth to the story of Lincoln's assassin. Readers will also learn of the aftermath of the assassination and get some possible answers to still unanswered questions related to the tragedy.

"Thus, Always to Tyrants", is still the Commonwealth's motto, but it never applied to Lincoln. Discover why Booth was so wrong by reading, Fortune's Fool.

title: Stephen Greenleaf is a very literate mystery writer
raw_text:
The writing was so great in this book that I found myself reading sentences over again just to savor the language. This is my second Greenleaf book, and it is great to know that I have at least half a dozen more awaiting me (assuming the rest are as good as the two I've already read).
The plot involves Greenleaf's lawyer-turned-private investigator, Marsh Tanner, returning from San Francisco to his Iowa home town to discuss what to do with the family farm. Two of his brothers want to sell it (but to whom -- coal strip miner, wildcat oil company, neighboring farmer, the town?), whereas his sister wants to keep the land in the family and let her daughter and SIL farm it.
Not long after Marsh arrives in town, however, his bad-boy nephew is found hung -- although it appears to be suicide, Marsh has reason to question this verdict. He starts poking around, and in the course of poking around, learns a lot of things about the people of his home town that had been kept secret.
Greenleaf's characters are vivid and memorable, and I was kept guessing about what happened to nephew Billy until the final chapter -- but it all made sense.

title: I expect more from you, Charlaine Harris
raw_text:
This review contains some spoilers.
I love the Sookie Stackhouse series. Charlaine Harris is my favorite author; however, Dead in the Family was an extreme disappointment. Somehow the story flat-lines. Unlike the other books, something is missing.
Now that Sookie is with Eric their relationship has become somewhat humdrum. Harris creates no memorable scenes between these two characters. We all remember Book four's shower scene between Sookie and Eric. We remember Book One's cemetery scene with Bill and Sookie. Readers expect romance involving vampires to be passionate and fiery. There are no such scenes in "Dead in the Family."
There seems to be no active contender against Eric for Sookie's love. Sookie as a female protagonist is still a strong character. She has become a lot edgier after being tortured by the fairies. There were a lot of minor characters that seemed unnecessary like Kennedy and Danny. There wasn't enough character development with Judith and Ocella. Season characters like Sam, Bill, and Jason didn't shine in this book. Claude, the gay Fairy, is an extremely bland character who is neither lovable nor humorous. The incorporation of Hunter seemed more like filler material that an integral element. "Dead in the family" touched very little on Vampire politics and just moderately more on werewolf politics. Of course it wouldn't be a Charlaine Harris story without the standard mysteries like the dead body found in yard and the unidentified fairy. The climax of the book is when the little Romanov vampire Alexei goes insane and attacks everyone, including the unidentified fairy. This would hardly be climactic when compared to vampire wars, werewolf and witch wars, fairy Wars, and bombings from the Fellowship of the Sun.
Will the next book delve into the politics with the Vegas vampires? Will the Fellowship of the Sun start attacking shifters and Weres? Maybe Charlaine Harris is running out of material and will have to incorporate more supernatural creatures like fallen angels, demons, or ghosts which are becoming popular topics for young adult literature. Much inspiration can already be drawn from the unpredictable nature of vampires, werewolves, and crazy religious humans.
Please let the next book be better than this.

I'm not using this text as a sole resource, however.  It's clear from the introductory matter that you already need to know some Arabic or Arabic linguistics or both to find your bearings.  But I find that a book such as Smart's "Teach Yourself Arabic" relies too much on an "inductive" method and the intelligence and good will of the reader.  Learning a language isn't the same as doing a mathematical proof.  If anything, the next best thing to immersing yourself in the language's culture is having a book that contains literary matter from which you can deduce certain truths about the language's structure and the culture of its speakers.  Plus, I find the author's non-Atlantic background to be refreshing.  (He's from India.)  Arabic is a complex language and culture, and any presentation of it will be partial and distorted, depending on the circumstances of the presenter's culture.  "Arabic for Beginners" is a valuable supplement to other English-language teach-yourself materials on Arabic.

title: The Best Way to Prep
raw_text:
The daunting task of preparing, shopping, and cooking a big meal overwhelms you. Perhaps you cook for a large family. A greater amount of food and kitchen space is required in an economy where more multi-generational families live together. Maybe you are a volunteer chef, or you are planning to open a small business. Richard Helweg breaks down bulk cooking and prep for the reader.

Before jumping into recipes, author Helweg reveals the secrets to planning. Take an inventory of food and equipment needed for your kitchen. Divide food into categories such as dairy and meat. Set aside time to prepare your inventory, shopping list, and to store food. Helweg's book prepares you for the fact cooking a meal in bulk takes a lot of work beyond the meal. In addition to inventory, Helweg writes about the importance of storing away food immediately and why you need to keep your kitchen clean.

Helweg also answers one of the most important questions foodies, readers, and home cooks want to know. What can I freeze? How long can I freeze this food for? Will the food retain its taste? The author covers everything from storage options to thawing food. Since food prices are going up at grocery stores and markets due to both the economy and nationwide drought, Helweg offers a guide; an opportunity for readers to assert independence whether it is for family, volunteering, or as a business owner.

title: THIS FORD'S TOP OF THE LINE VEHICLE

In my opinion, Ford's INDEPENDENCE DAY is the finest American novel of the nineties.  In this work, Ford brings back his everyman, Frank Bascombe.  As with Updike's Rabbit in RABBIT IS RICH, Frank has acquired wealth.  He has quit sportswriting, and he is currently peddling real estate.  Of course, his ex-wife is now married to a richer man, and Frank is still struggling to cope with his contemporary life.  His friends, his lover, his business associates all play their parts in his life.  As the holiday weekend approaches, Frank plans a trip with his son to the Hall of Fame, in the hope of helping his troubled boy straighten out.  Events intervene, and Frank again finds himself fighting to cope with his role in this world.  INDEPENDENCE DAY is Richard Ford's masterpiece.

title: WHERE IS THE FOLLOW UP???
raw_text:
I too purchased the original edition and was absolutely floored by well, everything. Easily the most complete and readable of all the books ever written on the Beatles. But for crying out loud, it has been SEVEN years! All this time that we have been waiting for the next volume, apparently Mark has been spending on a vastly more expensive re-write of Volume One. I mean, really?
I saw the Beatles live in their second to last concert in Seattle in 1966. I'll be 70 next month. Not to be complaining or anything, but speaking for myself I would have rather see the continuation of the story from where we left off at the end of the first book. If this really is a 3 volume series, how about giving your readers the last two books before you go re-writing the first?
I love the way you write about my favorite band, Mark, but please stop dangling the carrot and deliver the goods!
The Five Star rating above is for the original book, not the new and very expensive Love Me Do-Over. Just so we are all on the same page....as it were. Heavy sigh.
Richard Pennant
Hoquiam, WA

title: Meat for a thylacine fan
raw_text:
Science geeks, thylacine fans, travel daydreamers and scat fetishists will love this book. Scrap that. Anyone who enjoys good writing will enjoy this book. The geeks, thyfans, travel nuts and scatologists will just be jealous. The assorted imagery of current Tasmania -- sounds, smells and sweat -- are as appealing as the discriptions of roadkill are not. The tales of the Tasmanian tiger are heartbreaking, not just because I've been like, so totally into this critter since I was like, 8 or something, but because there is no reason whatsoever for said critter to be extinct. The frustration of that, and the urgency and passion of their hunt to add to the lists of sasquatch-esque thylacine sightings are tangible throughout. And the artwork is as poignant as it is gross. Both poignancy and grossness leave goosebumps.

Manditory quibble so I don't sound like a cheerleader: The various puns, often while involving minor fish-out-of-hemisphere tales of New Yorkers in the bush -- not as good as they might have seemed in the rough drafts. But then again, I just wanted more images of Tasmanian devils eating their way, tuchus-first, through various pademelon corpses. I'm single-minded that way.

The final result is, again, a very worthy-of-your-time book. But you'll read it fast, and want more. Might I suggest a follow-up hunt for the Steller's sea cow?

title: My goodness, this book was slow! And talky!
raw_text:
It reminded me of sitting around visiting with people that you like but who aren't all that interesting to listen to. There's certainly a coziness to the small Virginia town of Crozet and its inhabitants (two and four-footed), but a little less philosophizing and explaining particular topics and a little more action would have been good.

Maybe I need to quit reading this author's books. The drawings of animals in the book are absolutely adorable, but I found myself bored by all the animal conversations.

And I'm not convinced that fox-hunting is as benign a sport as the author apparently believes.

I'd tell you about the plot, but there's not much to say. Basically it involves two people who contract a very rare disease (how did they get it?)-- one of whom was actually murdered before the disease he was infected with killed him, the other of whom dies of the disease-- and thoroughbred horses -- these men were partners starting up a horse-breeding business. Were both these deaths murders? Related? Do horses have something to do with this? Who killed them?

Sadly, at least as much attention is paid in this book to the future of Harry, the overqualified post-mistress who may not be able to take her cats and dog to work with her any more and who is very unhappy about this. Then there's her relationship with her ex-husband, who is interested in getting back together with her. And a series of gossipy Virginia parties for the reader to attend...

I guess you either find this small town and its inhabitants charming enough to make up for the very slow pace or you don't.

title: What A Good Mystery Should Be
raw_text:
This item was given to me for my review.
Louise Penny has written another BRILLIANT mystery. How The Light Gets In possesses all the elements of the vert best kind of mystery, and Penny is always a tough act to follow when I look for other books to read. In her latest novel, Penny takes the reader back to the village of Three Pines which is the setting for most of her other Armand Gamache novels. Three Pines and its residents create an atmosphere that has a lot of us secretly wishing it were not just a work of fiction. I absolutely love the eclectic and eccentric cast of characters Penny has gathered in that village. However, Penny avoids caricature in developing her characters, and writes them as unique and highly appealing people.
Penny draws Gamache into Three Pines on one case and keeps him there as the issues of political corruption and police intrigue play out. The underlying threat within Gamache's own police force has been a growing plot thread in previous novels, and Penny often uses a chase within a chase to keep the reader guessing. The book is extremely suspenseful without resorting to gratuitous violence, and it proved to be an "all nighter" novel, with subsequent sleep deprivation. I suggest starting it on a Friday, if you wish to make it into work on time.
Penny excels on so many levels and in so many areas. Her dialogue is crisp and tight yet witty and engaging. She is able to capture the subtleties of character without giving in to wordiness, and she can keep the reader hooked from the first page to the end with seeming ease. I finished the novel feeling satisfied, but I was sorry it ended. In this novel, certain issues were resolved, but others were left open. I pray there are more Gamache novels in the works.

title: Perfect!
raw_text:
Edit: My review refers to the L.A. Theaterworks production.

I've seen many productions of this play on film, stage and radio and this is, far and away, the best production ever. A different, more English tone takes this production a million miles away from the well known film version and, charming though Rex Harrison et al are, this is all the better for being different.

Ian Ogilvy shines as the misogynistic Charles who carries a torch for his first wife despite his best efforts. Rosalind Ayres is fine as the slighted Ruth, playing it with a wonderful, indignant tone. But the undisputed star of the show is Judy Geeson who plays the mischevious Elvira with such wonderful drawling tones it's a delight to listen to her. I only wish we heard the word 'beastly' more in conversation!

Of my many audio books, this is absolutely my favourite but wonderful as it is, I'm just sorry that this was radio and not stage or screen. What a fabulous production it would have been.

I received a free copy of this book from Celebrate Lit, and these are my honest thoughts about it.

***

Esther's review:
I didn’t know what to expect when I picked up Cathe Swanson’s latest book. I loved the other two from her that I’ve read in the past, and this one was also good. It might not have been my favorite, partly because it felt roughly put together in some ways, but the story itself was good.

Having had grandparents that were involved in the hippy movement back in the day, I found that portion of this story fascinating. To see how they tried (and failed, in some cases) to work together—and why it didn’t work—was quite interesting. And to have a snapshot—even if it is brief!—of how Jesus works in those circumstances was really special.

I also loved seeing the two mother/daughter relationships change through the story—the humbling, giving process that occurs. It’s not the kind of thing you see all that much in books, necessarily, and watching the Lord work in their hearts was special.

I enjoyed Season of Change, and I’m looking forward to reading any sequels that come out. title: A skillful cohesive narrative of unexpected twists and turns
raw_text:
T. Martin Bennett’s beautiful, well-told human drama unfolds over a period of 9 years and spanning over millions of square miles of the globe as he captivates his readers about war games where one is ‘taught to predict the unpredictable and expect the unexpected’ (p.190). Bennett takes his readers through a spellbound experience of unpredictable & unexpected twists and turns of a cohesive narrative in Wounded Tiger.

Often, war stories overly focus on a single narrative of triumph. Yet, Bennett pulls out of the ashes of Hiroshima, the missing chronicle of the loss of millions including all who lost even their life to ever speak again. In his narrative, Bennett gives the reader a gift—to witness the loss and to wrestle with the deep meaning and hidden chronicles of war as well as the significance of life.

The women’s truth left Fuchida speechless.

“What can you possibly take from me that I haven’t already lost?”

“He saw that they weren’t just the words of a hopeless old woman, they were the words of an enraged nation, furious for having been led into a war that had devastated their country, a land they loved, a nation that had been ground into the dirt in humiliating defeat. She was the voice that was never heard by the military commanders when they passionately argued for war, and she was the voice of the millions who would never speak again. “ (P.361)

Fuchida squarely faces the hidden narrative, previously not considered. He was changed by the devastation and even by the untold loss of so many.

Martin Bennett skillfully crafts the three-stranded tale of captor and prisoner, a pair of airmen fighting on opposite sides, and a forgotten missionary daughter. He does so with such mastery of pacing, surprises, reversals, and timing that the book for me was a rapid page-turner unlike any other nonfiction novel.

Furthermore, Wounded Tiger is charged with the opportunity to consider the courage of forgiveness, the beauty of true freedom from hatred, and the dignity of all mankind.

title: Sadly redundant
raw_text:
This memoir was given to me for my review.
Let me set the record straight. I really enjoy memoirs of people learning to overcome life's difficulties and gain insight. I chose Pieces of My Mother: A Memoir because it was based on a topic I understand well, a girl learning to live without her mother. The book began on the sad day when Melissa Cistaro's mother got into her car and just drove away, never to permanently, or even frequently, return. Cistaro does a good job of capturing that moment and every miserable vignette she shares afterward. I feel for her because she DOES get how sad and confused and hurt she is as a child trying to understand a broken mother. There were some moments when the author could find common ground with her mother as an introvert in the middle of mommy-burnout, but as a mother who loved enough to stay and hurt, it is obvious that there are some things that neither the author, nor this reader, can totally understand. Cistaro shares how her mother's leaving not only affects her, but, also, her brothers Eden and Jamie. This aspect of the book is well established in flasbacks showing small cruelties, self blame, and the need to cling, as well as references to current alcohol and drug abuses. The flashbacks are well written, but begin to feel like a rehash of the same theme. When she puts in the part about the kittens in the buckets, I had to set the book aside for a while, then skip ahead. I hate the book. I hate the total misery of reading it. I know the book description says it is "haunting yet uplifting," but it was an "uplifting" desert for me. How do you rate a book that you wish you did not need to finish? I don't feel like there is much more to say about the author's mother than that she was obviously an addict with emotional problems, and that is sad, but I think her ex-professor had it right when he said she was a bit of a con, as well. Again and again the flashbacks tell the story. She is broken, got it. Cistaro is, also, broken, though by the chapter Clear Lake, she makes the conscious decision to turn her life around. But, that is the end of the book. Hopeful? For her, yes, but I struggle to say I would suggest the memoir to others. If the purpose of the book is to help the reader see her mother's dysfunction and the disastrous consequences, then that was established. But, a whole book of sad scene after sad scene? Perhaps it was cathartibut for the author. I hope so.

title: in the fine tradition of mystery writing
raw_text: I look forward eagerly to every new volume from Spencer-Fleming.  Throughout each narrative, she manages one or more intriguing plot lines, resolved by book's end, but there's also a continuing storyline that has arced from volume to volume.  The two main characters are admirable in their strengths, but compellingly human, and as sleuths, they're usually a couple of steps ahead of me.  There's a bit of "character torture" here; in the fine tradition of mystery writing, it wouldn't do to give them a happily-ever-after in Book One.  However, the author doesn't overwrite; Diana Gabaldon and especially Elizabeth George could learn something from Spencer-Fleming's control of her prose.

title: You have to be kidding
raw_text:
This is a book that reflects the power of self-promotion.

As the author will (and repeatedly does) tell you, he is considered an expert on poker. For all I know, he may be one. Unfortunately, that expertise is not presented in this book, which constitutes a somewhat disjointed collection of essays that rarely reveal anything that a reasonably thoughtful player would not already have figured out.

The author's apparently-favorite words: "obviously" and "clearly" [often as the lead-in to a statement with superficial validity but having some subtle theoretical weakness]. Favorite phrase: "It seems like..." (or "it doesn't seem...") Favorite sentence: some variation on "As I wrote in my book [fill in name of other book by same author]."

The self promotion quickly wears thin, as his 41 (I hope I didn't miss any) references in the text to other books include 36 to those he, or sometime coauthors David Sklansky and Ray Zee, wrote. The list of recommended books in the appendix constitutes nine books, of which seven are by himself or those coauthors; more can be found in the supplemental list.

But this weakness would be tolerable if the book offered insights that would improve a typical reader's game. Unfortunately, it doesn't. His strategic recommendations are unsupported and often at odds with good high-level strategy; his opinions on win rate and bankroll may be correct but are unsupported by data or mathematical proof; his opinions on good and bad games and on player types are probably correct but not novel to anyone who has thought beyond the shallowest level about the game. He devotes considerable space to an argument that limit hold-em is a more complicated game than no limit, but the argument is based on an extremely superficial look at the intricacies of the latter game -- for all I know his conclusion is correct (though I disagree), but as with most of his opinions it is essentially unsupported herein.

Don't fall for the hype; don't buy this book just because you've heard of the author.

title: West Virginia Hiking Trails
raw_text: WV Hiking Trails is not the first book by Allen deHart that I have read, and it certainly is not his best. Allen can describe a trail or a patch of forest with the best, there is no argument. This book is no exception. Where WV hiking trails misses the mark is the hasty organizing of the maps section. The trail descriptions do not refer you to the specific map(s) for the trail. This leads you to backtrack through the book searching for the right map for the trail you are reading about. This can be a real problem if using the map to find a trail head. The maps are also too small to use as trail maps or highway maps. My belief that this edition was put together in a rush and the editors  didn't spend enough time reviewing the maps section. I suggest you buy his Hiking Guide to the Monongahela National Forest instead.

title: Not up to Proulxian standards!
raw_text: I have been a fan of Annie Proulx for years ... ever since discovering her with one of her wonderful stories in The New Yorker.  I have bought every one of her hardcovers since then, (short of How To Make Apple Cider!), and have enjoyed them, especially her Wyoming stories, since I come from and went to high school and College in Wyoming and worked at Eatons Ranch, out of Sheridan, for many years.  Her last two books I was disappointed with: the dark and gloomy. "Accordian Crimes", and now the hopeless "Bird Cloud", which I so looked forward to, I bought it in advance.  Here Annie buys land in southeastern Wyoming, without surveying it's year-round weather conditions ... the County doesn't plow her road in the winter, so she's either snowed-in or out! Then she endeavors to build a glitzy, fussy home more suited to the Hamptons than the North Platte, and spends the balance of the book whining about it's cost over-runs, and construction difficulties in the boondocks. Luckily, she's wealthy from her literary output, so she pours hundreds of thousands to tart the place up with hopelessly fussy accutrements and deluxe furnishings, a Japanese soak tub, polished concrete floors she keeps changing the colors of, amid countless architectural mistakes ad nauseum, to where I just didn't care any more.  Her main descriptive largesse involves the bird population thereabouts, worrying about the eagles nesting, as well as the neighbors' cattle marching down the creek onto her property.  Some of her descriptions are wonderful, and vintage Proulx, but she lost my interest when the basic story (if there even IS one) of a wealthy single woman pissing-away millions of dollars building an inappropriate luxe house in a country more suitable to a nice log-cabin.  Now I hear the place is up for sale for $3.7 million.  Good luck to her in this market!  I hate to think that Annie Proulx, in her eighties, may have her best material behind her.

title: The great western exploration told as only Ambrose can
raw_text:
Undaunted Courage is a must read or listen for anyone interested in exploration and history. As Ambrose highlights, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark made a remearkable journey up the Missouri River to find a "direct and practical" passage to the Pacific ocean and the western part of America. It is clear Ambrose has a true understanding of what Lewis and Clark must have experienced during thier two and one hlaf year journey.
Doctor, outdoorsman, taxidermist, writer and diplomat, Lewis comes to life in this remarkable journey that Ambrose tells us in Undaunted Courage. Ambrose provides the reader a great flavor for the immensly productive Lewis and Clark expedition. Not only does the pair find a route to the West, but they documented several hundred new species of plants and animals and created, if only for a short period, diplomatic relations with the various Indian tribes along the way. Undaunted Courage is a great title for this amazing trip.
Ambrose gives us the post expedition difficulty Lewis goes through. For such a great master of a variety of things, it is hard to understand why Lewis is unable to get his life on track after the expedition with so many great opportunites available to him. Unfortunately, there is no insight provided as to why Lewis is unable to more readily function in the aftermath of the expedition. This was the one piece of the book that left me wondering.
For a great trip up the Missouri, read this one and enjoy it.

title: Out-of-focus Rebecca---Villain or Victim?
raw_text:
Ever since I read Du Maurier's "Rebecca" as a young girl, I fantasized about the vivid character of Rebecca, who never makes a physical appearance throughout the whole story, yet manages to drive the action of all the players. Having glimpsed her essence, I wondered about her motivation--her real motivation--not the prejudiced opinions gleaned from the other characters. What had brought this glamorous female graced with "brains, beauty and breeding" to her less than glorious end at the murdering hand of her own supposedly smitten husband? How had her childhood injected her with the concentrated need to be mistress of Manderley?
If you are expecting all the answers from Sally Beauman's novel, "Rebecca's Tale", look elsewhere. Rather than a straight-forward account of Rebecca's story in Rebecca's voice, we get instead---in an attempt by the author to utilize Du Maurier's masterful yet underhanded heresay approach to uncovering Manderley's secrets, another go at more opinions--and these from two characters who were not even in Du Maurier's classic and do little to elicit sympathy or interest from the reader. Divided into four sections (each narrated by a different voice), the plot centers around the appearance of Terence Grey to the Manderley district. For very personal reasons, Grey is stirring up the old scandal/drama of the first book in order to seek some thread of the elusive Rebecca. Chief on his list of interviewees is Colonel Julyan, now a man in his 70s and his daughter, Ellie. Paramount to Grey's scheme to weed out the truth is the delivery of an old notebook seemingly written in Rebecca's own hand.
So, Rebecca does indeed get to speak, but through a diary written towards the end of her life to her unborn child. Even the information found here is questionable as Rebecca is touted as liar and performer who will say what she will to get what she wants. The "why" is still seeped in mystery and Rebecca sadly remains a shadowy image like film that has not quite been developed.
Ultimately, this lack of substance disappoints even though for the most part the story itself could be compelling if it left out the annoying angst of Ellie's feminism, Julyan's guilt and Grey's inability to be true to himself. Such "modern" "politically correct" dilemmas, have no place in a period piece set in the early 50s. Yes, all the "live" players' issues are resolved, but these events, while tying up the plot's loose ends again do not quite work within the context of discovering the real Rebecca.
On the positive side, Beauman does a wonderful job of weaving her rather labyrinthine tale with the use of the four distinct voices. Her tone works well in conveying the misty Cornwall coast as it carries with it that unsure quality that Du Maurier adopted initially while allowing the young and inexperienced second Mrs. De Winter to meander through her daydreams while dealing with the testy events of her story. Also interesting is the premise of Rebecca's childhood as related through the journal, even though again this is not developed to its full potential, but rather takes the easy way out by remaining slightly elusive. The appearance at the end of the second Mrs. DeWinter seemed too convenient; her characterization was silly--after living through the events of all three Manderley related tales (yes, the plot and outcome of Susan Hill's "Mrs. De Winter" is also incorporated into this story)there is no way this woman could remain so gauche.
As the Du Maurier estate has sanctioned this book as a sequel, I recommend reading it to all of you who hold "Rebecca" dear as one of the great Gothic masterpieces of the 20th century. Who knows, maybe the next one will have all the definitive answer!

title: Learning about Panama
raw_text:
This book offers a thorough description of Panama up through 1995. It focuses on history from 1968-1995, as well as a description of how Panama's economy developed, as well as its society, religion, environment, military, politics and American influence.

A more recent book by one of the authors gives more depth on the history of US domination: John Lindsay-Poland also wrote Emperors in the Jungle: The Hidden History of the US in Panama (2003).

Among the many things readers will learn are these:

* The president is elected directly (no electoral college) to a five-year term, and he appoints the Supreme Court and the governors of the nine provinces.

* The legislature is unicameral, one house, and consists of 72 deputies.

* Omar Torrijos is the most important political figure in the nation's history, and his movement is referred to as torrijismo.

* Women didn't win the vote until 1946, and still face sexist barriers.

* After the 1989 US invasion, the US State Dept's human rights report (1994) identified Panama's principle problems as prolonged pretrial detention, an inefficient & often corrupt judicial system, and overcrowded, oppressive prisons.

* The ease of corporate registry facilitates one of the world's largest merchant fleets, with thousands of ships registered in Panama and flying the Panama flag.

* Bananas are the biggest export crop.

* More than seven in ten Panamanians call themselves Catholic, though fewer than one of five of them regularly attend Mass.

* Though blacks are more integrated socially than in some other nations in the region, they nonetheless are still widely considered second-class citizens and have fewer job opportunities. This second-class treatment stems back to racial segregation and a two-tier racial wage system established by the US in the Canal Zone.

* The Guna have been the most successful indigenous peoples in the world in preserving their land and culture.
Their geographic isolation in the San Blas islands is one reason.

* While Panama hosts an abundance of tropical flora & fauna, the country also faces severe environmental problems of deforestation, erosion, overfishing, and lack of water.

Though dated, the book remains interesting for those seeking to understand the dynamic Central American country. It could use an new, updated edition.

title: The King: Bratva Blood
raw_text:
The King is the first book in S.R. Jones’ series, Bratva Blood. In this book, Ms. Jones continues the romantic journey between Cassie Evans and Konstantin Silvanov. She further delves into their personalities revealing their vulnerabilities. She also provides a more in depth investigate into the intricacies of a crime family revealing the constant threaten of take overs. In this book, Konstantin wrestles with his conscious and fights his inner demons regarding his feelings for Cassie. Likewise, Cassie does the same. Konstantin seeks revenge for the brutal murder of his wife. With his crime family, he uncovers every stone to find out who was behind this heinous act while simultaneously battling the chaos of his personal life. He seeks security for his stepson, Michael. When outside threats endanger the ones he loves, what does Konstantin do? Will he be able to keep them safe? Can Cassie cope with his lifestyle? You must read this book to discover their journey.

I like Ms. Jones’ use of a dual-prong plot line. One prong is Cassie and Konstantin’s romantic journey. The other is the suspense of who is behind the plot to take down Konstantin. Ms. Jones’ does a remarkable job creating dialog. The internal monologues provide snippets of understanding into each character’s backstory. I liked how she balanced high-tensioned scenes with amusing ones. She does this through dialog. Her descriptive scenes capture the readers’ attention drawing them into the story. Ending with a cliff hanger is also a nice touch. Well done, Ms. Jones!

raw_text: Hide & Seek was excellent! Much different I think from Patterson"s standard way of writing.  He typically never seems to focus a lot on character development. He gives you the thrills and chills without overloading with back-stories and points of view. This novel however has been different.  The story had depth (more than usual), character development, and a good mystery that slowly revealed itself up to the very end. The story is told from the first person viewpoint of the main character Maggie. It's also told in third person about Will. During the first and third person stories, there are flashbacks that build on character development. Of course in typical James Patterson fashion, there's always a healthy dose of disturbing imagery and offensive language, but not to the point it's ever too much (he's nowhere as bad as Jack Ketchum). He can however tell a great story. The quality of his storytelling is still there in this one, but much better! I would like to see Patterson write more novels like this. I can ready anything by Patterson. He isn't the best writer, but an excellent storyteller. I thoroughly enjoyed this story. This was written right around the time he stopped working and became a full-time writer. Well-done! 5 stars!

title: Overwhelming Sadness--A Must Read
raw_text: As a novelist with my debut novel in its initial release, I am fascinated by this glimpse of one of my all-time favorite authors nearing the end of his career.  Richard Brautigan's suicide nearly two decades ago haunts American literature almost as darkly as Hemingway's does from four decades ago.  In AN UNFORTUNATE WOMAN, the reader can see where its author is heading.  I'm glad this book has finally found print, but I'm sad knowing full well how the life of one of my literary heroes will soon end.  Brautigan's final work tells, in journal form, of a man's journey following the hanging death of a friend.  In some ways, it's a typical, rambling, fun Brautigan book.  At certain points the man shines like he did at his best.  It's the Sixties and Seventies all over again.  At other points, sadness takes over, as one can see a magnificent talent fading.  AN UNFORTUNATE WOMAN is a book I'm glad I read, and I would freely recommend it to everyone.

title: Astrophysicist tracks the Star of England
raw_text:
Author Mark Anderson was a young whippersnapper in '93, fresh out of grad school with an MA in astrophysics, when he first heard about the so-called "Shakespeare problem." A devotee of scientific method, he was bemused by the reaction of otherwise rational people who became "irrational and redfaced" whenever the words "earl of Oxford" were uttered in concordance with 'Shakespeare'. "Having concentrated on theoretical physics," he writes, "I was most interested in what makes a theory work, what kinds of evidence support a theory, and what kinds of evidence modify or negate a theory." He undertook his investigation, in short, as a rhetorical exercise.

This allowed him a refreshing freedom to imagine and conjecture, to think outside the box of orthodoxy --even Oxfordian orthodoxy -- to arrive at some startlingly creative theories about who the real Shake-speare was and what deep and very human conflicts -- personal and political -- his famous Works were working out. I agree with critics here who believe he grew obsessed ("fell in love") with his subject along the way, but how could he not? That's what happens in every good detective story. In any case, his makes a much more likely and engaging story than the bland one put forward by most Shaksper religionists.

I say this even though I confess that underneath I remain a traditionalist at heart. I prefer the Gentle Will I grew up with, just as I prefer the blemishless Jesus put forth in the Gospel of John. But Anderson's heretical theories have not undermined in the least my passionate response to the film, SHAKESPEARE IN LOVE, another intelligent writer's attempt to connect the "real" Shakespeare with the genesis of his work. It's all just a public conversation we're having, and Anderson's well-researched contribution is exciting, thought-provoking, and welcome.

John Slade

Director, Theatre Arts

Ojai Performing Arts Theatre Academy

Whose side are you on?

John Mak

title: Timeless, a true classic
raw_text:
The Prince is a strange work. It was not written as as a book at all, and was certainly never intended for general publication. Niccolo Machiavelli was the Secretary of State to the Florentine Republic in Renaissance Italy. That Republic was overthrown by the Medici, and the senior officials were beheaded or driven into exile. Machiavelli was fortunate enough to survive. Years later, old and sick, he wanted to return. As a peace offering, he did a cut and paste on a much earlier work he had written called the Discourses. It was a study of all the governmental styles that had been attempted in history, and why they succeeded or failed. The condensed version dealt only with autocracy. He dedicated the manuscript to Lorenzo the Magnificent and sent it to him.

Sadly, Lorenzo never saw it and Machiavelli died in exile. The manuscript was found years later by scholars examining Lorenzo's papers. They published it. Many people are shocked by it's ideas yet the rival princes and condotieri used just those ideas to survive in the vicious politics of the Renaissance. The rulers of the day may have been patrons of the arts, but they were quite dangerous as well.

I wanted the best version available, and this is it.

title: A well written story that is a captivating page turner
raw_text:
Even if you have no stake in the Lancaster community, this book could be an entertaining read because of the way the story was told. If nothing else, Pressed is intriguing as a well told and well documented story of "how the sausage was made" in a private-public redevelopment project. Voyeuristically, I enjoyed reading this credible retelling of a chapter of Lancaster’s history, about which I have no inside knowledge.

I had been deeply involved in the Lancaster civic, political and business community a couple of decades prior to the time of this story, so I was well acquainted with many people who are actors in the book’s story. The characteristics of the individuals as portrayed in the book are generally consistent with their personalities as I knew them.

I disagree with many of Commissioner Henderson’s political views. Before reading the book, I wondered if it might be a self-serving fiction, but instead I found it to be credible as an important historical effort. Commissioner Henderson cannot be dismissed as a feminist who was on an ego trip to use her power as the leading Democrat in Lancaster County to frustrate Lancaster’s good old boys’ club.

This book convinced me that, as bipartisan politicians, Commissioners Henderson and Shellenberger acted courageously in what they honestly perceived to be their constituents’ best interests to question, and even attempt to obstruct, the Penn Square Partners use of Lancaster County taxpayers to absorb the risk of a real estate development project that was rubber stamped by too many.

I was not surprised that the editorial teams of the Lancaster Newspapers compromised the reporting of unvarnished truth by their manipulation and distortion of facts to make their headlines and news stories more scintillating. Partisan slants between the Democratic Intelligencer Journal and the Republican New Era had long been practiced. I was disturbed to see that the editorial writers had raised the stakes from yellow journalism, intended mostly to stimulate sales of more newspapers, to the intentional character assassination of an individual whose opinions and actions threatened the value of the Lancaster Newspapers’ real estate holdings. After reading the book, I conclude that the Lancaster Newspapers’ executives and editorial staff were guilty of what Commissioner Henderson claimed.

Perhaps the most important conclusion from Pressed is not that Commissioners Henderson and Shellenberger were victims, or that the Penn Square Partners were self-centered power mongers who were promoting an ill-conceived project. Future historians will have an opportunity to evaluate whether the completed Penn Square project is successful as a crown jewel that gives the Lancaster economy and culture a competitive advantage. However, Pressed gives those future historians the documentation to debate the effect of the power of an unbridled local media to spin the political agenda of a community, as Lancaster Newspapers did for decades up to and culminating with the Penn Square debacle.

I admit to feeling disappointment that Commissioner Henderson lost her lawsuit, so the newspaper principals who violated the public’s trust in the manner by which they attacked her were not required to pay for the damage they caused. Yet I also feel somewhat saddened that time has eroded the drama and power of the local media to the extent that holding the Lancaster Newspapers accountable today is like beating a dead horse that was outraced and trampled by social media and cable news.
